"Stop emitting carbon"

"Well, we've decided that doing so would cost us $10,000,000B in profits. Pay us that as a fine!"

I've always advocated that governments should introduce laws that affect companies' profits slowly. For example, here in Australia, I supported the carbon tax, but thought it should be incrementally introduced over a decade (in practice it was introduced all at once but with so many exemptions that it wasn't that disruptive to companies in the end). This is because governments need investor confidence. Investors need to be assured that the government won't suddenly change things and make their investments unprofitable. Lower investor confidence means that investors won't invest in the next big government project, because they don't trust that they will be protected if the political landscape changes.

Governments, and the public, need investor confidence. Sometimes, this might mean paying a billion dollars to an evil company. But if that means that more than a billion dollars gets invested in good economic growth because of the increased confidence, then this can be a good thing all up.

So I say, when you realise that an industry is doing something bad, but not illegal, go ahead and make it illegal. When they sue, pay up. That's the cost of progress. To say "Too bad" to the investors in the 'evil' industries will hurt good industries too. Establishing that companies are not at fault if the law changes seems like a pretty good standard to have.

Essentially the government is acting as an insurer against companies losing profits due to law changes. Ideally the cost of this 'insurance' should be paid by companies through tax, so that's what I would advocate.

Private insurance companies won't cover "the law changed", so it's up to governments if they want people to do business with confidence.

So yes, I've advocated that laws should be changed slowly so as to keep confidence high. But changing them quickly and simply paying out the people who lose out seems like a great way to accelerate legal change whilst not hurting investor confidence.

No, this is meant for security. I.e. if your application doesn't actually check that the HTTPS certificate from a site is valid, it will borrow code that does check for that from another application.
